extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of Canadian/colonial history; readers interested in the Northwest Mounted Police and the 1885 Riel Rebellion
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length historical narrative recounting the Northwest Mounted Police's operations during the 1885 Riel Rebellion and the subsequent period of reconstruction, emphasizing leadership, tactics, civil protection, and policing duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of civilians as first duty
rubrics_metrics.description: “The people there must be protected as a first duty.” Also expressed as the British maxim of 'women and children first.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text frames decisions (e.g., holding Prince Albert rather than joining offensive operations) around prioritizing protection of settlers and non-combatants over seeking battlefield glory. Abandoning civilian population centers is criticized as un-British and inhuman; protecting refugees in churches and stockades is presented as the overriding obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and willingness to face odds
rubrics_metrics.description: The Police are described as having a record of 'not counting odds when duty seemed clear' and as men 'who had no thought of self when fighting was the duty of the hour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valor and steadfastness under severe numerical disadvantage (e.g., Duck Lake, Cut Knife) are presented as core virtues; the narrative emphasizes that, in proportion to numbers engaged, more Mounted Police were killed or wounded than any other body except one battalion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to hold posts and provide refuge (staying at assigned stations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mounted Police 'stayed at their posts or moved from place to place, as required in a readjustment period' rather than dispersing after Militia withdrawal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity of presence—guarding stations, relieving refugees, maintaining order during the post-conflict reconstructive period—is treated as essential police work distinct from militia campaigning and crucial to long-term stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of diplomacy, tact and influence to prevent uprisings
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers used 'patience, skill and tact' and influence with chiefs (e.g., Mistawasis) to keep many Indians from joining the rebellion; Superintendent Cotton's 'diplomatic' restraint is singled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non‑military measures—personal diplomacy, relationships with missionaries and local leaders, recruiting loyal chiefs and organizing escorts/tours—are presented as vital to preventing and healing conflict and should be pursued alongside military action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gathering legal evidence and ensuring due process after conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: After the rebellion the Police were to 'gather the evidence, to secure the presence of witnesses, to furnish guards' so that rebels 'should be rounded up and dealt with by process of law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-conflict policing includes investigative and legal-support duties to ensure insurgents are lawfully tried; this civil-legal role is key to preventing future lawlessness and to demonstrating state justice (examples: trials of Riel and other rebels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of local knowledge and scouts
rubrics_metrics.description: The text stresses the value of men 'who knew the country and the Indians at first hand' and recounts capture of Riel by local Police scouts (Tom Hourie, Armstrong, Diehl).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of terrain, local languages, tribal politics and inhabitants is a decisive operational advantage; commanders should use local scouts and men with frontier experience when planning movements or pursuing insurgents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership qualities for commissioners and senior officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissioners are noted for traits such as 'foundation building, discipline, organization,' impartiality, 'wide human sympathies,' courage, administrative ability, 'intuitive insight,' rapid assimilation of facts, and expectation that 'orders [be] carried out with exactness and dispatch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective senior leadership combines administrative skill, fair-mindedness, military courage, local understanding, decisiveness and the ability to synthesize documents/facts quickly; these qualities enable both successful field operations and institutional rebuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical judgment in deciding when to engage or refrain
rubrics_metrics.description: Irvine's decision to hold Prince Albert instead of joining Middleton is defended: not leaving civilians exposed outweighed joining the seat of war; McKay would not be drawn into a fight at Duck Lake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Savvy commanders must weigh civilian-protection responsibilities, odds, and strategic consequences before engaging; apparent opportunities for battlefield action should be balanced against broader duties and the likely effects on civilian populations and recruitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination with militia and higher command, and mutual respect
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative highlights friction and missed opportunities between General Middleton and the Mounted Police, but also records high praise (Earl of Minto) that police presence changed operational burdens—'the fact of Colonel Irvine's force being at Prince Albert afforded a safe refuge to many outlying settlers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrated planning and mutual appreciation between regular military forces and local police units are presented as important; underestimating local forces can impair campaign outcomes while their presence can have decisive moral and practical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical engineering and logistical ingenuity in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Major Perry's improvisation—throwing a rope, building a swinging raft and later a ferry to cross a flooded Red Deer River, commandeering lumber, and personally leading dangerous crossings—is recounted as exemplary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field commanders should be prepared to solve engineering/logistical problems creatively, personally supervise hazardous operations, and ensure safe transit of men, guns and supplies; such practical initiative can enable entire columns to proceed where otherwise stalled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term reconstruction, patrol and settlement support
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-rebellion duties included patrolling a vast territory, guiding and protecting settlers, encouraging Indians to remain on reserves and helping half-breeds adapt from nomadic life to settled agriculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police roles extend beyond immediate security to reconstruction: continuous patrols, administrative oversight, and social policies to stabilize populations and integrate newly exposed regions into peaceful settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and recording of sacrifice and service
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. A. Jukes' report praised the 'humble tribute to the courage and fortitude' of the Mounted Police and noted their high casualty rate relative to numbers engaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate record‑keeping, public recognition, and institutional remembrance of service and sacrifice are important for morale and for justifying the corps' role and actions to the wider public.
